title: Light Shoe or Proper Boot? Where Salomon Hiking Shoes Fit on Kenyan Trails
meta_title: Salomon Hiking Shoes in Kenya: 5 Comfortable Models Compared
meta_description: Salomon hiking shoes for Kenyan trails: X Ultra, Quest and Speedcross compared, fit tips, buying thrifted pairs and where to find them in Nairobi.
excerpt: Salomon hiking shoes are light, grippy and great for Kenyan day hikes. Here is how the X Ultra, Quest and Speedcross compare, how they fit and what to check on a thrifted pair in Nairobi.
featured_image_alt: Salomon hiking shoes – a hiker wearing Salomon trail shoes outdoors
content:
A low-cut Salomon X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX weighs about 370 g per shoe, which is why Salomon hiking shoes suit Kenyan day hikes such as Ngong Hills, Mt Longonot and Hell's Gate. They grip dry rock and dust well and need little breaking in. For heavy packs on Mt Kenya, a stiffer boot works better.

Plenty of Nairobi hikers own Salomon hiking shoes already, often bought for the gym or the school run, and wonder whether they will cope with a real mountain. Others spot a thrifted pair and are not sure which model they are holding. Below we explain the main Salomon lines, how they fit, which Kenyan trails they handle well, what to check on a pre-owned pair, and where to find them in Nairobi.

Quick Facts

  • Brand: Salomon was founded in 1947 in Annecy, in the French Alps, and is now part of Amer Sports.
  • Flagship hiking shoe: the X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX, at about 370 g per shoe (low) or about 455 g (mid).
  • Multi-day boot: the Quest 4 GORE-TEX, a leather and textile boot of about 650 g per boot, built for loaded treks.
  • Mud specialist: the Speedcross 6 trail runner has 5 mm Mud Contagrip lugs and a 10 mm drop.
  • Fit: snug heel and a fairly narrow forefoot; the X Ultra 5 also comes in Wide versions.
  • Best Kenyan use: fast day hikes on firm or rocky ground, from the Ngong ridge to Longonot's crater rim.

Are Salomon Hiking Shoes Good for Kenyan Trails?

Yes, Salomon hiking shoes are a strong choice for most Kenyan day hikes. They are light, grippy on dust and rock, and comfortable from the first walk. Their limits show on long, loaded treks and in deep forest mud, where a heavier boot or a lugged trail runner does better.

Salomon's footwear grew out of trail running, and you can feel it. Compared with a classic leather boot, Salomon hiking shoes flex more at the forefoot, sit lower to the ground and encourage a quicker stride. On a 13.5 km loop of Longonot's crater rim, that means less weight lifted with every step. On the grassy, sometimes slippery descent off the Ngong Hills, the Contagrip rubber bites well as long as the ground is not deep clay.

The trade-off is support. A low-cut shoe leaves the ankle free, and a softer chassis lets more of a sharp rock come through underfoot. If you carry a light daypack and walk on firm ground, that is a fair exchange. If you plan to haul 12 kg up the Sirimon route, it is not.

Where do Salomon hiking shoes fall short?

Salomon hiking shoes struggle most with heavy loads, deep mud and long descents on loose scree. A low X Ultra will not stop scree pouring in, and its lugs clog faster than a dedicated mud shoe in Kiambu's red clay during the short rains.

Wet forest in the Aberdares is another tough test. Bogs there can swallow a low shoe to the ankle, and once water comes over the collar a GORE-TEX lining simply holds it in. For that kind of trail, pair your Salomon hiking shoes with waterproof leg gaiters or choose a mid-cut.

Which Salomon Models Are Worth Knowing?

Four Salomon lines cover almost everything a Kenyan hiker needs: the X Ultra (low and mid hiking shoes), the X Ultra 360 (a simpler sibling), the Quest (a proper trekking boot) and the Speedcross (a trail runner built for mud).

X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX: the all-rounder

The X Ultra is the model most people mean when they talk about Salomon hiking shoes. According to Salomon's X Ultra 5 GORE-TEX product page, the low version weighs 13 oz (about 370 g) per shoe and combines a GORE-TEX membrane, an All-Terrain Contagrip outsole, an advancedChassis insert for lateral support, an EnergyCell EVA midsole and a Matryx upper woven with Kevlar for abrasion resistance.

It closes with Quicklace, Salomon's one-pull lacing system, and the spare lace tucks into a pocket on the tongue. Salomon lists it for rocky, technical and mixed terrain on full-day hikes. In Kenyan terms, that is Hell's Gate's gorge, the Ngong ridge, Kereita Forest and Longonot on a dry day.

X Ultra 5 Mid GORE-TEX: more cover for the ankle

The mid version weighs about 16 oz (roughly 455 g) per shoe and uses regular laces through traditional eyelets instead of Quicklace. The higher collar keeps grit and puddle splash out and gives a little more support when you step off a rock awkwardly.

For Kenyan hikers who want one pair for both the dry season and the short rains, the mid is often the safer bet. It is still light enough for the Ngong Hills but copes better with wet grass and the loose ash on Longonot's descent.

X Ultra 360: the simpler sibling

Among Salomon hiking shoes, the X Ultra range currently includes the X Ultra 360, sold in plain, GORE-TEX, mid, Edge and leather versions, and usually priced below the X Ultra 5. Think of it as an easy-going hiking shoe for lighter use. The non-waterproof versions breathe better on hot, low trails such as Karura or Oloolua in January.

Quest 4 GORE-TEX: the trekking boot

The Quest is Salomon's answer to the classic backpacking boot. The Quest 4 GORE-TEX has a nubuck leather and textile upper, a GORE-TEX lining, a 4D advancedChassis for stability, a protective toe cap and mudguard, and a gusseted tongue. At about 650 g per boot, it is listed for multi-day hikes on mixed, alpine terrain.

Among all the Salomon hiking shoes and boots, the Quest is the one we would point to for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro. It handles a full pack, frozen ground before dawn and the scree below Point Lenana at 4,985 m far better than a low X Ultra.

Speedcross 6: the mud runner

The Speedcross is a trail-running shoe, not a hiking shoe, but it turns up on Kenyan trails often enough to deserve a mention. Salomon lists the Speedcross 6 at 11 oz (about 310 g) with 5 mm Mud Contagrip lugs, a 10 mm drop and Quicklace. Those deep chevron lugs bite into wet clay better than the X Ultra's shallower tread.

For a fast morning on a muddy Ngong ridge in November, a Speedcross can feel surer underfoot. It has less protection from sharp rock, though, and the soft lugs wear quickly on tarmac, so do not use it for the walk to the matatu stage every day.

How Do Salomon Hiking Shoes Fit?

Salomon hiking shoes usually fit snugly, with a locked-in heel and a fairly narrow forefoot. Hikers with average or slim feet tend to like Salomon hiking shoes; hikers with wide feet often find the toe box tight unless they choose a Wide version.

Salomon calls its fit system SensiFit: the upper wraps the foot from the midsole up to the laces, and on the X Ultra 5 and Quest 4, "Active Support" wings help hold the foot in place. In practice this gives a precise, close feel that suits quick, technical walking. The X Ultra 5 is also sold in Wide GORE-TEX versions, low and mid, which is useful if other Salomon hiking shoes have pinched your little toes.

Should you size up for Kenyan hikes?

Many hikers go half a size up in Salomon hiking shoes when they wear thick hiking socks or face long descents. Try both sizes if you can, and choose the one where your toes do not touch the front on a downhill step.

Kenyan descents are steep and long. Coming down Longonot's crater wall or the final kilometres off Ol Donyo Sabuk, your foot slides forward with every step, and a shoe that felt perfect in the shop can bruise toenails by the car park. Leave about a thumb's width in front of your longest toe. The size label inside the tongue usually lists several systems, so note your size in centimetres as well as EU or UK, because it travels between brands more reliably.

Quicklace: love it or swap it

Quicklace is fast and tidy, but it tightens evenly along the whole foot, which some hikers find hard to fine-tune. If you have a high instep, you may prefer the mid or Quest models with traditional laces. On any pair, push the lace lock into the tongue pocket so it cannot snag on brambles or rock.

Which Salomon Shoe Suits Which Kenyan Trail?

Match Salomon hiking shoes to the hardest hour of your hike, not the easiest. Dry, firm ridges suit the low X Ultra; wet grass and loose ash call for the mid; deep mud suits the Speedcross; and anything above 4,000 m with a full pack calls for the Quest or a heavier boot.

The pattern is simple: the lighter the shoe, the more it depends on dry, firm ground. Our Mt Longonot hike guide explains why the crater descent is harder on footwear than the climb, and our post on boots for Kenyan trails covers what each type of ground asks of a sole.

Can you climb Mt Kenya in Salomon hiking shoes?

You can walk the lower stages of Mt Kenya in Salomon hiking shoes, but for summit night most hikers are better off in a warm, supportive boot like the Quest 4. Temperatures near Point Lenana drop well below freezing before sunrise, and light mesh shoes lose heat fast.

Some trekkers carry low Salomon hiking shoes as camp shoes and for the forest and moorland days, then switch to boots higher up. That works if you have a porter or space in your pack. If you are buying one pair for the whole climb, choose the boot.

Should You Buy Salomon Hiking Shoes Second-Hand?

Buying Salomon hiking shoes second-hand makes good sense, as long as the sole, midsole and lining still have life left. A lightly used X Ultra or Quest from a quality thrifted source costs far less than a new pair imported at full price.

That is the idea behind our shop: we sell quality thrifted outdoor gear plus some new items, so big-brand footwear becomes affordable for Kenyan hikers. Our post on thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi explains the wider approach. What matters with any pre-owned shoe is knowing what to look at before you pay.

What should you check on a pre-owned pair?

  1. Look at the Contagrip lugs under the ball of the foot and the heel. Rounded, smooth lugs mean the grip has gone, and most Salomon hiking shoes are not designed to be resoled.
  2. Squeeze the midsole at the heel. Deep, permanent wrinkles in the EnergyCell foam mean the cushioning is flattened.
  3. Twist the shoe gently. The chassis should spring back; a creak or a soft, floppy middle suggests damage.
  4. Check the Quicklace for fraying where it runs through the eyelets, and make sure the lace lock slides and holds.
  5. Feel inside the heel cup. Torn lining there causes blisters within an hour.
  6. Look for a GORE-TEX label if the pair is sold as waterproof, then flex the toe area for cracks along the crease.
  7. Try the shoes on with your hiking socks and walk down a step or ramp to test toe room.

How can you tell genuine Salomons from copies?

Copies of popular Salomon hiking shoes, especially the Speedcross, do circulate, so it helps to know the general signs. Genuine pairs usually have neat, even stitching, a cleanly moulded Contagrip or Salomon logo on the sole, a size label inside the tongue with a style code, and a firm, branded Quicklace lock.

A price far below what a used pair normally fetches is a warning in itself. None of these points proves anything alone, and a well-worn pair will show scuffs. Look at the whole shoe, and buy where you can handle it properly before paying.

Pro Tips for Salomon Owners

  • Knock the mud off early: clay dries hard in Contagrip lugs; rinse the soles with plain water the same evening.
  • Dry in the shade: stuff the shoes with newspaper and keep them away from charcoal jikos, heaters and hot car dashboards, which can weaken glue and foam.
  • Swap the insole, not the shoe: a flattened OrthoLite insole is cheap to replace and can bring back cushioning.
  • Pick the membrane by season: GORE-TEX for the long rains (March to May) and short rains (October to December); breathable versions for hot, dry months.
  • Mind the collar: on low shoes, add gaiters for Longonot's ash and Aberdares bogs.
  • Break them in anyway: walk 15-20 km around Nairobi before a big hike, even though Salomon hiking shoes feel comfortable from day one.

How Do Salomon Shoes Compare With Other Boots We Stock?

Salomon hiking shoes are lighter and quicker than the leather boots on our shelves, but less supportive under a heavy load. Keen suits wider feet, Lowa suits long treks, and Quechua suits tighter budgets.

The Keen men's Targhee Mid waterproof boots have a much roomier toe box than any Salomon, a rubber toe guard and a KEEN.DRY membrane, which makes them friendlier for wide feet in wet forest. The Lowa Renegade Evo GTX Mid is the pick for long, rocky, loaded days, with a nubuck upper and a stiffer frame than an X Ultra. And the Quechua waterproof hiking boot is the budget route into a membrane boot for the rains.

Our brand round-up of hiking boot brands for Kenya compares Salomon with Lowa, Scarpa, Keen, Merrell and others in one table, if you are still choosing a brand rather than a model.

Which socks work best with Salomon hiking shoes?

A medium-cushion merino or synthetic hiking sock works best, because Salomon's snug fit leaves little room for a thick, bulky sock. Our merino wool hiking socks stay warm when damp and help prevent the hot spots that a close-fitting shoe can cause on long descents.

Common mistakes when buying Salomons

The most common mistake is buying a Speedcross for hiking because it looks tough; it is a running shoe with soft lugs that wear fast on rock. Others include buying a low X Ultra for Mt Kenya summit night, choosing the usual size without testing a descent, and assuming every pair is waterproof. Only versions labelled GORE-TEX have the membrane, so read the tongue label before you pay.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Salomon shoes good for hiking in Kenya?

Salomon shoes are good for most hiking in Kenya, especially day hikes on firm or rocky ground such as Ngong Hills, Hell's Gate and Mt Longonot. They are light, grippy and comfortable without much breaking in. For deep mud choose a lugged Speedcross or add gaiters, and for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro with a full pack choose the Quest boot or another supportive trekking boot.

Do Salomon hiking shoes run small?

Salomon hiking shoes often feel snug rather than small, with a close heel and a fairly narrow forefoot. Many hikers stay at their usual size, while those with wider feet or thick socks go up half a size or choose the X Ultra 5 Wide. Always test on a slope: your toes should not touch the front when you step down.

Is the Salomon X Ultra waterproof?

The Salomon X Ultra is waterproof only in its GORE-TEX versions, marked "GTX" or "GORE-TEX" on the tongue or side. Non-GTX versions breathe better but let water in. Even a GORE-TEX X Ultra can fill up if water or mud comes over the low collar, so use gaiters or a mid version for bogs, river crossings and heavy rain.

Can I hike in Salomon trail running shoes?

You can hike in Salomon trail running shoes such as the Speedcross on short, light-pack day hikes, and their deep lugs grip well in mud. They give less protection and support than a hiking shoe, though, and the soft rubber wears faster on rock. For regular hiking, an X Ultra is the better long-term choice.

How long do Salomon hiking shoes last?

Salomon hiking shoes last until the Contagrip lugs wear smooth or the midsole foam flattens, which depends on how often you hike and on what ground. Rocky Kenyan trails and daily city walking wear soles faster than forest paths. Rinse off mud, dry them in the shade and swap tired insoles to get the most use from a pair.

Final Thoughts

Light feet make for happy long days, and that is what Salomon does best. For dry ridges and rocky day hikes around Nairobi, a low or mid X Ultra is hard to beat; for mud, a Speedcross grips harder; for Mt Kenya, the Quest boot earns its extra weight.

Whichever you pick, buy Salomon hiking shoes for the trail you will actually walk, with room for your toes on the way down.
